extraction.name: PIQA: Physical Interaction Question Answering
extraction.description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. The dataset consists of multiple choice question answering pairs where a model must choose the most appropriate solution to a physical goal from two options. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with an additional 2K and 3K held out for development and testing respectively. The dataset is inspired by instructables.com and focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
extraction.citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI 2020.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) annotators who were prompted with links to instructables.com. Annotators were asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and construct two component tasks, articulate a physical goal and a valid solution, and then provide a permutation (trick) to their own solution which makes it invalid. Annotators were seeded with instructables drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g. special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of commonsense.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions and goals were sourced from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair. Annotators used these as inspiration to construct goal-solution pairs.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data. AFLite performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose given feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large and compute embeddings of all remaining instances. An ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data determined whether pre-computed embeddings were strong indicators of the correct answer option.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Goals were tokenized by Spacy. The GPT BPE tokenizer was used for solution tokenization. The longest 1% of the data was removed for analysis. AFLite algorithm was applied to remove annotation artifacts. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite. During model experiments, examples were truncated at 150 tokens, affecting 1% of the data.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided prompts derived from instructables.com. They were asked to: (1) provide a physical goal often centered on atypical materials, (2) provide a valid solution for achieving the goal, and (3) provide a trick - a permutation of their solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was run prior to the main annotation stage where annotators had to successfully identify (>80%) well-formed and underspecified goal-solution pairs. Validation HITs were also run after the main annotation stage. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. An interface with a diff button was included to highlight where solutions differ.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement during validation were removed from the data. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. Annotators chosen for human performance evaluation achieved 90% on the qualification HIT. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm (using BERT-Large embeddings), Spacy (for tokenization)
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' ability to understand physical commonsense knowledge, which is critical for applications such as robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors argue that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world to eventually be communicated with language, and that language models relying solely on text are limited in capturing physical world knowledge.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Reporting bias was identified as a challenge during data collection, where annotators tended toward prototypical solutions and common tools. The instructables prompting approach was used to flatten the distribution of referenced objects and address this bias. AFLite was applied to remove annotation artifacts that could artificially inflate model performance.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on English only. Models trained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance by finding large sources of in-domain data, but this does not reflect true physical understanding. The dataset may not capture all dimensions of physical commonsense knowledge. Some correct examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge were removed during validation.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for benchmarking and evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. It can be used for training, validation, and testing of NLP models. It can also serve as a diagnostic tool to probe the physical knowledge of deep pretrained language models. The dataset is split into training (16,000+ pairs), development (2K pairs), and test (3K pairs) sets.
